title: Supply Chain

post.author: u/tilthaven_seeds_berenike
post.title: I sort returned seeds at night. At 00:55 our patch sheet said ALL CLEAR. At 03:05 the label laptop said jotlog 3.4.0.

blocks.text: I'm Berenike, night volunteer at the Tilthaven Seed Library. People borrow seed packets in spring and bring back seeds from their harvest in autumn. I sort the returns at night and keep an eye on our small catalogue site.

The site is seven services: small programs that each do one job (as in The Assembly Line). Catalogue, search, loans, returns, members, reminders, and labels, which runs on a laptop beside the label printer. None is written from scratch. Each uses libraries: ready-made code that other people write and share, like buying a part instead of making it.

Libraries use other libraries too, like a seed mix: you choose one packet and get many kinds of seed. The libraries a service asks for by name are its direct dependencies. The ones that ride along inside them are transitive dependencies.
Each service keeps a dependency file: the list of libraries it asks for by name.
To build a service, a tool fetches the listed libraries, then packs them with our code into one bundle. That bundle is what runs.
Libraries come in numbered releases called versions, and we pin each one: the file names one exact version, never "newest", so nothing changes by surprise.
Our written rule: a serious flaw gets patched, swapped for a fixed version, within 24 hours.

At 21:30 on Tuesday 13 October, the desk laptop chimed with an email from the makers of jotlog, a popular logging library. A log is a service's diary of what it did, and jotlog writes it. Versions 3.0.0 to 3.8.2 had a serious flaw, fixed that evening in 3.8.3. A stranger could run their own instructions on any computer running a flawed copy, from outside, with no password.

Which of our services had it? Nobody could say. I rang Oluchi, our volunteer developer, at 21:42. She searched each service's dependency file for jotlog: 12 minutes a service, 84 minutes in all. At 23:06 she had an answer: loans and members. She patched them one after the other, 50 minutes each.
Her patch sheet: each line shows a service, what its dependency file says, and its state.

loans      jotlog 3.8.1 listed   patched to 3.8.3, 23:56
members    jotlog 3.6.0 listed   patched to 3.8.3, 00:46
catalogue  not listed            not affected
search     not listed            not affected
returns    not listed            not affected
reminders  not listed            not affected
labels     not listed            not affected
00:55      ALL CLEAR, Oluchi
Labels restarts every night at 03:00 to load tomorrow's labels, and I check its first lines on the laptop. The first line is always jotlog saying hello with its version. At 03:05 it said 3.4.0.

Achille built labels in May 2023, when that laptop had no internet. He copied jotlog's own package, 3.4.0, the newest that spring, by hand into the service's folder, so every built bundle carried it, and no list named it. I rang Oluchi straight away. Labels was patched at 03:55.

diagram.aria: The night from 21:00 on Tuesday 13 October to 05:00 on Wednesday 14 October. The jotlog flaw is announced at 21:30. Loans runs a flawed copy until it is patched at 23:56, members until 00:46. The patch sheet says ALL CLEAR at 00:55. Labels runs its bundled copy, 3.4.0, until 03:55; the copy was seen at 03:05.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the patch sheet and the labels start-up lines. The flaw was announced at 21:30. Loans ran a flawed copy until 23:56 and members until 00:46. The sheet said ALL CLEAR at 00:55, while labels ran its bundled 3.4.0 until it was patched at 03:55.

blocks.text: On paper, every door was shut at 00:55. One stood open until 03:55.
The volunteers meet on Saturday, and I get one change to propose. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Two questions before you choose. Where did 3.4.0 live, if no list named it? And what do search's own libraries use? Some teams keep an SBOM, short for software bill of materials: a parts list of every library inside a built service, made by a tool at each build. Others say the dependency file is enough.

replies.author: u/tilthaven_seeds_berenike
replies.text: In its own folder inside the labels bundle. And search: this morning Oluchi opened the dependency file of sievekit, the search helper library it uses. sievekit uses jotlog 2.9.1, older than the flaw. Harmless, by luck. Nobody had looked.

comments.author: u/source_of_truth_jacinda
comments.text: The dependency file is the source of truth. If a library is not listed, it is not in the service; that is what the file is for. Your search was right. Labels was one person breaking the rules in 2023. Keep searching the files, and ban copies by hand.

comments.author: u/tilthaven_dev_oluchi
comments.text: I'm the developer. If every library took its newest version every night, 3.8.3 would have reached loans and members by itself at 02:00, with no search at all.

comments.author: u/edge_rules_aukje
comments.text: I work for the firm whose computers run your site. We sell a web firewall: a guard in front of every service that reads each request coming in (a message asking a service to do something) and blocks ones that match known attacks. We had a rule for the jotlog flaw from 23:40. Yours is switched off.

reply.prompt: The volunteers meet on Saturday. What one change should Berenike propose? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Keep a parts list of every library in each built service, so one search finds all.
options.part2: From Saturday, every build makes an SBOM, a parts list of every library inside the built bundle, kept beside it. In the sim I chose search an SBOM made from each build and replayed the night. One search across all seven parts lists answered in 4 minutes, at 21:46: jotlog in four services, three affected. Labels showed up too, because the list is made from what was built, not from what was asked for, and search's 2.9.1 showed up marked not affected. Patched one after the other: loans 22:36, members 23:26, labels 00:16. The longest exposure falls from 6 h 25 min to 2 h 46 min, and the total from 12 h 07 min to 5 h 48 min. We kept pinning and the 24-hour rule, and labels now names jotlog in its dependency file like everyone else.
options.senior: Answer "are we affected?" from what was built, not from what was asked for. A dependency file is a wish list; an SBOM made at every build is the parts list, transitive libraries and hand-copied ones included, so one search over all of them answers in minutes. OWASP's A03 asks for exactly this: track direct and transitive dependencies, and manage an SBOM of your entire software. Keep pinning and patch deadlines beside it; the SBOM tells you where, the deadline tells you how fast.

options.text: Update every library to its newest version every night, so nothing old is ever left.
options.verdict: Newest is not the same as safe
options.part2: We set every library to take its newest version at 02:00 each night. In the sim I chose newest every night and replayed the night. Oluchi had already patched loans and members, at 23:56 and 00:46; the 02:00 update would have brought 3.8.3 to both anyway. But labels' copy is on no list, so no update touched it: still 3.4.0, found by chance at 03:05, longest exposure still 6 h 25 min. And the 30 nights before show the cost: 3 builds broken by libraries that changed, and on Saturday 26 September the reminders service took mailkite W, a release its own makers withdrew as unsafe 2 days later.
options.senior: Taking the newest of everything, untested, swaps one risk for two. New versions change how things work and break builds, and a trusted project's new release can carry something harmful, as xz utils did in March 2024. Updates also reach only the libraries a list names. Pin, update on purpose with tests, set patch deadlines by how serious a flaw is, and know what is really inside each build.

options.text: Search each service's dependency file for the library's name and patch what turns up.
options.part2: We kept the dependency file search. In the sim, search each dependency file replays the night as it happened: 84 minutes to answer, at 23:06; jotlog seen in 2 services; the sheet says ALL CLEAR at 00:55 while labels runs 3.4.0. Labels was found by chance at 03:05 and patched at 03:55, 6 h 25 min after the email. The search never saw search's 2.9.1 either; it was harmless only because it was old. A dependency file lists what was asked for, not what was built.
options.senior: A dependency file is a list of intentions. It names direct dependencies, and nothing that rides along inside them or was copied in by hand. Banning hand copies helps but never proves there are none. Search what was built, and treat "not listed" as "not known", never as "not there".

options.text: Put a firewall rule in front of every service to block the new flaw's known requests.
options.part2: We switched on the hosting company's web firewall and its jotlog rule. In the sim I turned the rule on: from 23:40 it blocks requests that match the known pattern. Every exposure stays the same, 12 h 07 min added up over the three services, because the three flawed copies are still inside until each is patched, labels until 03:55, and labels, on its laptop in the library, never sat behind the firewall at all. Requests that differ from the known pattern pass, and the rule says nothing about where the flaw lives.
options.senior: A firewall rule is a good first hour: it can cut the easiest attempts while you patch. But it matches only shapes it already knows, others get past, and the flawed copy is still inside. Use it to buy time, never in place of finding and patching every copy.

sim.title: Replay the jotlog night at the Tilthaven Seed Library
sim.lede: You're Berenike, replaying the night from 21:30 on Tuesday 13 October, when jotlog's makers announced a serious flaw in versions 3.0.0 to 3.8.2. The figures are given data: seven services, each with two libraries in its tree; jotlog sits in four of them, and the labels copy, 3.4.0, is bundled by hand and named on no list. Choose how you look (each dependency file, or an SBOM, a parts list made from each build), the update policy (pinned with a 24-hour patch deadline, or newest every night), and the firewall rule, then replay the night.
sim.tryThis: Try this: replay as found. The dependency file search takes 84 minutes, sees jotlog in 2 services, and the sheet says ALL CLEAR at 00:55 while labels runs 3.4.0 until 03:55. Now search an SBOM made from each build: 4 minutes, 3 affected found, labels patched at 00:16, longest exposure 2 h 46 min. Try newest every night: labels is untouched, and the 30 nights before show 3 broken builds and a release its makers withdrew as unsafe. Last, turn the firewall rule on: exposure stays 12 h 07 min.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the patch sheet was false about what it searched. It searched the dependency files, the lists of what each service asks for, and labels ran a copy of jotlog that no list named. Answer "are we affected?" from a parts list made from every build, an SBOM, and the bundled copy shows up in minutes.

steps.title: Your libraries' flaws are your flaws.
steps.text: A service is mostly other people's code. It asks for a few libraries by name, its direct dependencies, and each of those brings its own, the transitive dependencies. A flaw in any of them runs inside your service with all of your service's rights; that is dependency risk. A supply-chain attack goes one step further: someone plants something harmful in a library many people use, and it works because every service that takes the library trusts it as its own code. OWASP's Top 10:2025 lists this whole family as A03, Software Supply Chain Failures.

steps.title: The wish list and the parts list.
steps.text: A dependency file says what a service asks for. A lockfile (The Assembly Line) adds the exact version of everything fetched, transitive ones included. Neither knows about a library copied in by hand. An SBOM is made from the build itself. First, the build fetches the libraries and packs the bundle. Second, a tool reads what is really inside the bundle, every library with its name and version, wherever it came from. Third, it writes that down as the SBOM and stores it beside the bundle. What can go wrong: code pasted line by line, without its package, may carry no name or version for the tool to read.

steps.title: Are we affected? in minutes, step by step.
steps.text: First, read the notice: which library, which versions are flawed, which version fixes it. Here, jotlog 3.0.0 to 3.8.2, fixed in 3.8.3. Second, search every SBOM for that library, one search across all of them. Third, mark each match affected or not by its version: search's 2.9.1 is older than the flaw, so it is not. Fourth, patch the affected services, rebuild, and check the new SBOM shows the fixed version. In the sim this took 4 minutes instead of 84, and labels was patched at 00:16 instead of 03:55. What can go wrong: a service that has not been rebuilt has an old SBOM, so rebuild or rescan it.

steps.title: Pinning, update policy and patch deadlines.
steps.text: Pinning names one exact version, so nothing changes by surprise, but pinned versions grow old unless someone updates them. An update policy says how: on purpose, with tests, on a routine cycle. A patch deadline says how fast for a serious flaw: here 24 hours. Taking the newest of everything every night is not safer: in the sim it broke 3 builds in 30 nights and took mailkite W, a release later withdrawn as unsafe. In March 2024 a trusted project, xz utils, shipped a new release with harmful code hidden inside, so "always take the newest" is no shield either.

steps.title: Firewall rules buy time.
steps.text: A web firewall reads requests coming in and blocks those that match known attacks. On the night of a new flaw, a rule for its known pattern is a sensible first step while you look. It does not remove the flawed copy, it misses requests shaped differently, and it never sees anything that starts inside. In the sim, the rule changed no exposure: 12 h 07 min, added up over three services.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for Saturday. Top row: the build, which fetches libraries and packs them; the built bundle, what really runs; the SBOM, a parts list made from the bundle at every build. Bottom row: the flaw notice naming jotlog 3.0.0 to 3.8.2; one search across all seven parts lists, about 4 minutes; patching within the 24-hour rule, for the 3 services found.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for Saturday. Every build packs a bundle, and a tool lists what is really inside it as the SBOM. When a flaw notice arrives, one search across all seven parts lists finds every copy, bundled ones included, in about 4 minutes, and the 3 affected services are patched within the 24-hour rule. Replayed, labels is patched at 00:16 instead of 03:55.

fix.title: The fix: an SBOM from every build, one search, and a patch deadline
fix.text: Make an SBOM at every build of every service, from the built bundle, and keep it beside the bundle. When a flaw is announced, search all of them at once, mark each copy affected or not by its version, and patch the affected services within the deadline, checking each new SBOM shows the fixed version. Keep pinning, update on purpose with tests, and name every library in its dependency file, so a hand copy like labels' becomes a listed one. Use a firewall rule only to buy time while you patch. In the sim, the SBOM search answers in 4 minutes instead of 84, finds 3 affected services instead of 2, and cuts the longest exposure from 6 h 25 min to 2 h 46 min.

limits: An SBOM is only as good as the tool that reads the bundle. A library copied whole, with its own package, usually shows up; code pasted line by line may carry no name or version and slip past.
An SBOM describes one build. A service that has not been rebuilt for months has an old list, so rebuild or rescan old services too, and keep the lists where one search reaches them all.
Finding is not fixing. Someone still has to read the notices, and each patch here took 50 minutes; three services in a row took until 00:16.

explain.seniorTake: Most of what runs in a service was written by someone else, so a flaw in a library is a flaw in your service. The question on the night is always "are we affected?", and the honest answer comes from what was built, not from what was asked for. Make an SBOM at every build so one search finds every copy, direct, transitive or bundled by hand. Pin versions and update them on purpose with tests; set patch deadlines by how serious a flaw is. Don't trust "newest" as a policy, because a trusted project's new release can carry harm too, and treat a firewall rule as time bought, not as a fix.

realWorld.title: Log4Shell, December 2021: CISA's guidance
realWorld.text: CISA wrote of "active, widespread exploitation of a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability" in the Apache Log4j logging library, known as "Log4Shell." In plain words: "An unauthenticated remote actor could exploit this vulnerability to take control of an affected system."

realWorld.title: CISA: find every copy
realWorld.text: "Organizations need to perform comprehensive analysis to fully enumerate all Log4J vulnerabilities." Enumerate means list every one; that is the question an SBOM answers.

realWorld.title: NVD CVE-2021-44228: the versions and the score
realWorld.text: The NVD's record begins "Apache Log4j2 2.0-beta9 through 2.15.0 (excluding security releases 2.12.2, 2.12.3, and 2.3.1)". It was published on 10 December 2021 with a base score of 10.0, CRITICAL, the highest.

realWorld.title: NTIA, 2021: what an SBOM is
realWorld.text: "An SBOM is a formal record containing the details and supply chain relationships of various components used in building software."

realWorld.title: OWASP Top 10:2025, A03
realWorld.text: "Software supply chain failures are breakdowns or other compromises in the process of building, distributing, or updating software." Its advice includes: "Centrally generate and manage the Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) of your entire software." and "Track not just your direct dependencies, but their (transitive) dependencies, and so on."

realWorld.title: xz utils, March 2024: newest is not safe either
realWorld.text: The NVD's record CVE-2024-3094 begins: "Malicious code was discovered in the upstream tarballs of xz, starting with version 5.6.0." Tarballs are the packed release files; the harm came in a trusted project's new release.

realWorld.title: The same question for AI: LATENT, Poisoned Wells
realWorld.text: LATENT's Poisoned Wells builds on this case.

asked: A serious flaw is announced in a common library: how do you know within an hour whether you are affected?
How do you handle transitive dependencies?
interview.answer: I'd want an SBOM, a software bill of materials, made automatically at every build from the built artifact, listing every library with its version: direct dependencies, transitive ones, and anything bundled. Kept in one place, it turns "are we affected?" into one search: read the notice for the library and the flawed versions, search every SBOM, mark each match affected or not by version, then patch in order of exposure and check the new SBOM shows the fix. A dependency file alone isn't enough: it lists intentions, not what shipped, and misses hand-copied code. For transitive dependencies, commit a lockfile so builds are reproducible, let the SBOM show the whole tree, and when a fix sits deep in the tree, update the library that pulls it in or override the version, then test. Around that: pin versions, update on purpose with tests rather than taking the newest every night, and set patch deadlines by severity, hours for a critical flaw. A firewall rule buys time on the first night but doesn't remove the flaw. A story I'd tell: a seed library's patch sheet said all clear at 00:55 while one service still ran a hand-bundled copy of the flawed logging library until 03:55; an SBOM search would have found it in 4 minutes.

terms.def: The seed library in this story. People borrow seed packets in spring and bring back seeds from their harvest in autumn. Berenike is its night volunteer.
A library that lends seeds instead of books. You borrow a packet, grow the plants, and return some of the seeds they make.
Tilthaven's website for finding, borrowing and returning seeds. It is made of seven services.
A small program that runs on its own and does one job for the others. Tilthaven's seven are catalogue, search, loans, returns, members, reminders and labels.
Ready-made code that other people write and share, which a program uses for one job, like buying a part instead of making it.
A library a service asks for by name in its dependency file. Loans and members ask for jotlog directly.
A library that comes along inside another library, not asked for by name. Search's jotlog 2.9.1 comes inside sievekit.
A service's list of the libraries it asks for by name. It says what was asked for, not everything that ends up in the build.
Turning code into something that runs: a tool fetches the listed libraries, then packs them with the code into one bundle.
The packed result of a build, the thing that actually runs. Labels' bundle carried jotlog 3.4.0 in its own folder.
A library copied into a service's own files by hand, so it rides in every build but no dependency file names it. Labels' jotlog 3.4.0, copied in May 2023.
A numbered release of a library, such as 3.8.3. Bigger numbers are usually newer.
Name one exact version in the dependency file instead of "newest", so nothing changes by surprise.
Swap a flawed version for a fixed one, rebuild and put it live. At Tilthaven each patch took about 50 minutes.
Oluchi's record of the night: each service, what its dependency file says, and its state. It said ALL CLEAR at 00:55.
How soon a flaw must be patched once it is known. Tilthaven's rule is 24 hours for a serious flaw.
A team's rule for when and how libraries move to newer versions: pinned and updated on purpose with tests, or the newest every night.
A mistake in code that can let someone do what they shouldn't. jotlog 3.0.0 to 3.8.2 had a serious one.
The popular logging library in this story (invented). Versions 3.0.0 to 3.8.2 had a serious flaw, fixed in 3.8.3 on 13 October.
A program's diary: one line for each thing it does, written as it happens, with the time first.
A library that writes a program's log for it. Most services use one, which is why a flaw in a popular one reaches so far.
The search helper library in this story (invented). The search service uses it, and it uses jotlog 2.9.1.
An invented release of the reminders service's email library, withdrawn as unsafe by its makers 2 days after it came out. The sim's nightly-update history takes it.
A library packed up for sharing, with its name and version inside. Achille copied jotlog's package into labels by hand.
Short for software bill of materials: a parts list of every library inside a built service, with versions, made by a tool at each build.
The plain name used here for an SBOM: what is really inside a built service, not what was asked for.
A file that records the exact version of every library a build fetched, transitive ones included (The Assembly Line). It does not see hand copies.
The finished, stored output of a build, labelled with what went into it. Here it is called the bundle.
The danger that comes with using other people's code: a flaw in any library, direct or transitive, runs inside your service with its rights.
Planting something harmful in a library or tool many people use. It works because every service that takes the library trusts it as its own code.
Running a flawed copy after the flaw is public. Here measured from the 21:30 email to the moment each service was patched.
A guard in front of a site that reads each request coming in and blocks ones that match known attacks. It does not remove a flaw.
A message sent to a service asking it to do something, such as show a page.
One instruction to a web firewall about what to block. The hosting company's rule for the jotlog flaw ran from 23:40.
A request shaped differently from the known one, which a firewall rule may not match.
The company whose computers run a website for a fee.
Someone who writes and looks after programs. Oluchi is Tilthaven's volunteer developer.
A widely used logging library from the Apache Software Foundation, for programs written in the Java programming language.
The name given to the serious Log4j flaw announced in December 2021, CVE-2021-44228.
Short for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a public id for one known flaw, such as CVE-2021-44228.
The US National Vulnerability Database, run by NIST, which publishes a record and a severity score for each CVE.
The NVD's severity score for a flaw, from 0 to 10. Log4Shell's was 10.0, CRITICAL.
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which published guidance on finding and fixing Log4j.
The US National Telecommunications and Information Administration, which published the minimum elements for an SBOM in July 2021.
A widely used set of tools for packing files small. In March 2024 its new release 5.6.0 was found to carry harmful code.
OWASP's public list of the ten weaknesses web applications most often get wrong (The Ten Doors). The 2025 list puts supply chains at A03.
A03 in the OWASP Top 10:2025: breakdowns or compromises in building, distributing or updating software, including flawed libraries.
An international standard for running information security. A.8.8 covers technical vulnerabilities and A.5.21 the ICT supply chain.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC7.1 covers finding vulnerabilities.
The main software that runs a computer and everything on it. A hosting company's computers carry their own.
One list of everything you run, at every layer: your own services, their libraries, and the systems you rent underneath them.
Everyone who supplies the information and communications technology you use: software makers, libraries, hosting companies.

atWork: Look for a library copied into a project by hand years ago: a folder of someone else's code inside your own, or a packaged file sitting next to your code. It is a common pattern, and no dependency file names it. Then ask three questions. Do we make an SBOM at every build, from the built artifact, and can one search reach all of them? How long would it take us, tonight, to answer "are we affected?" for a named library and version range? What is our written patch deadline for a serious flaw, and who reads the notices? Check old services that haven't been rebuilt in months too. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.8 (management of technical vulnerabilities) expects you to know your software and act on vulnerabilities in time, and A.5.21 covers managing security in the ICT supply chain; if SOC 2, criterion CC7.1 covers detecting new vulnerabilities and configuration changes. An SBOM per build, with dated patch records against a written deadline, is evidence for both. Build it in now, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: At 22:00 a serious flaw is announced in a widely used library, versions 2.0 to 2.6. Your company runs forty services. Your manager wants to know by 23:00 which ones carry a flawed copy, and how you'll be sure next time. What do you do?

keyIdeas.idea: Answer from a parts list made from each build, an SBOM, not from the lists of what was asked for
Include transitive and bundled copies, not only direct dependencies
Patch the affected services against a deadline, and check each new build shows the fixed version

recall.model: Don't trust the manifests alone: they list what each service asks for, not what shipped. Search an SBOM, a software bill of materials made from each built artifact, across all forty services at once; it lists every library and its version, so it catches transitive copies inside other libraries and anything bundled or copied in by hand. Mark each match affected or not by version, then rebuild the affected services against the patch deadline and confirm each new SBOM shows the fixed version. If we don't have SBOMs yet, start making one at every build tonight, so next time the answer takes minutes.

recall.prompt: What does an SBOM list that a dependency file usually doesn't?
options: Only the libraries a developer asked for by name
Every library really inside the built software, transitive and bundled ones included
recall.why: A dependency file is a wish list of direct dependencies. An SBOM is made from the build itself, so it lists what is really inside, including libraries that come inside other libraries and copies placed by hand. At Tilthaven it found jotlog in four services, not two.

recall.prompt: Why is "take the newest version of every library every night" not a safe update policy?
options: It breaks builds with untested changes, can take in a harmful new release, and never touches copies no list names
It is against the OWASP rules
Pinned versions can never be updated
recall.why: In the sim, nightly newest broke 3 builds in 30 nights and took mailkite W, later withdrawn as unsafe, and labels' bundled 3.4.0 stayed until 03:05. xz utils in March 2024 showed a trusted project's new release can carry harm.

recall.prompt: On the night of a new flaw, what does a firewall rule for its known pattern do?
options: Removes the flaw from every service
Buys time by blocking requests that match the known pattern, while the flawed copies stay inside
recall.why: The rule blocks only shapes it knows, and the flawed copies are still inside until patched. In the sim, turning it on left exposure unchanged at 12 h 07 min.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Every build at Tilthaven now makes an SBOM, and one search reaches all seven. In March a flaw was announced in a date library, and the search answered in 4 minutes: none of our services listed it. Two weeks later the hosting company wrote to say the computer running our services carries that same date library, in a version with the flaw, inside its own software. None of our SBOMs had mentioned it.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. How did the SBOM search miss it, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The SBOMs cover only what Tilthaven builds; the hosting company's own software sits outside them
Ask suppliers for their own SBOMs or vulnerability notices, written into the agreement
Keep one inventory across every layer, including the systems you rent, and search it on every notice

coldCase.model: The search was honest about what it searched: our SBOMs describe what we build, and the hosting company's software is not our build. A parts list only covers what it was made from. First, ask the hosting company for their SBOM or, at least, a written promise in the agreement to tell us within a set time when their software carries a known flaw; a supplier's software is still part of our supply chain. Second, keep one inventory across every layer we run on, including the operating system and anything rented, and search it on every notice, not only our own lists. Third, give supplier patches a deadline too, and check they met it.
